title: Dark Matter and Closure
lead: Stars and galaxies move as if there were far more matter than we can see. This section sets out the evidence for this dark matter, the critical density that would just halt the expansion of the universe, open, closed and flat universes, and what dark matter might be, from MACHOs to neutrinos with mass and WIMPs.
objectives: Discuss the existence of dark matter.
Explain neutrino oscillations and their consequences.
summary_html:
• Dark matter is non-luminous matter detected in and around galaxies and galactic clusters.
  • It may be 10 times the mass of the luminous matter in the universe, and its amount may determine whether the universe is open or closed (expands forever or eventually stops).
  • The determining factor is the critical density of the universe and the cosmological constant, a theoretical construct intimately related to the expansion and closure of the universe.
  • The critical density $\krhoc$ is the density needed to just halt universal expansion. It is estimated to be approximately $10^{-26}\;\text{kg/m}^{3}$.
  • An open universe is negatively curved, a closed universe is positively curved, whereas a universe with exactly the critical density is flat.
  • Dark matter’s composition is a major mystery, but it may be due to the suspected mass of neutrinos or a completely unknown type of leptonic matter.
  • If neutrinos have mass, they will change families, a process known as neutrino oscillations, for which there is growing evidence.
notes: The two problems the book leaves unkeyed are left out, and three things are kept as the book prints them: the speeds of the stars “should decrease as the square root of the distance” where inversely is meant, the problems sit under the header “Problems Exercises,” and WIMPs are called leptons; the muon and tau neutrinos, which the source sets with a Latin v, are set as ν.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s own key. Two of the four problems have no keyed answer and are left out: converting the critical density to eV/c² per cubic meter and finding the neutrinos per cubic meter that would close the universe, and the volume and radius the Sun would fill at the critical density. The four conceptual questions are unkeyed and carry AI-marked suggested approaches. No Check Your Understanding box is printed, so nothing is set inline.

figures.original_caption: Evidence for dark matter: (a) We can measure the velocities of stars relative to their galaxies by observing the Doppler shift in emitted light, usually using the hydrogen spectrum. These measurements indicate the rotation of a spiral galaxy. (b) A graph of velocity versus distance from the galactic center shows that the velocity does not decrease as it would if the matter were concentrated in luminous stars. The flatness of the curve implies a massive galactic halo of dark matter extending beyond the visible stars. (c) This is a computer-generated image of X rays from a galactic cluster. The X rays indicate the presence of otherwise unseen hot clouds of ionized gas in the regions of space previously considered more empty. (credit: NASA, ESA, CXC, M. exercises.prompt: Discuss the possibility that star velocities at the edges of galaxies being greater than expected is due to unknown properties of gravity rather than to the existence of dark matter. Would this mean, for example, that gravity is greater or smaller than expected at large distances? Are there other tests that could be made of gravity at large distances, such as observing the motions of neighboring galaxies?

answer.solution: A star in a circular orbit needs a centripetal force $mv^{2}/r$, which gravity supplies. If the speeds stay high far from the center while the luminous mass inside the orbit hardly grows, then either more mass is there than we see or gravity at those distances is stronger than Newton’s law gives for the visible mass: it would have to fall off more slowly than $1/r^{2}$, roughly as $1/r$, to keep the curve flat. The two explanations can be told apart by other tests at large distances: the motions of galaxies in clusters and of neighboring galaxies about one another, the bending of light by clusters (gravitational lensing), and cases such as colliding clusters where the mass that bends light is found separated from the luminous gas. A change in gravity would have to explain all of these at once in the same way, while dark matter can sit wherever the observations put it.

exercises.prompt: How does relativistic time dilation prohibit neutrino oscillations if they are massless?

answer.solution: A massless particle must travel at the speed of light. Time dilation slows a moving clock by the factor $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}$, which grows without limit as $v$ approaches $c$, so at $v = c$ no time at all passes in the neutrino’s own frame between its creation and its detection. A change of flavor is a process that takes time, so a massless neutrino could not change on the way; only a neutrino with mass, moving slower than light, has time pass for it and can oscillate.

exercises.prompt: If neutrino oscillations do occur, will they violate conservation of the various lepton family numbers ($L_{e}$, $L_{\mu}$, and $L_{\tau}$)? Will neutrino oscillations violate conservation of the total number of leptons?

answer.solution: Yes, they violate the conservation of each lepton family number: an electron neutrino has $L_{e} = 1$ and $L_{\mu} = 0$, so when it becomes a muon neutrino $L_{e}$ drops by one and $L_{\mu}$ rises by one. They do not violate the conservation of the total number of leptons, since one neutrino becomes one neutrino and the sum $L_{e} + L_{\mu} + L_{\tau}$ stays the same.

exercises.prompt: Lacking direct evidence of WIMPs as dark matter, why must we eliminate all other possible explanations based on the known forms of matter before we invoke their existence?

answer.solution: WIMPs are an entirely new form of matter, invented to explain the observations, and by their nature they are very hard to detect directly. An explanation that brings in something new and unseen should be accepted only when explanations using what is already known have failed; otherwise any puzzle could be answered by inventing a new particle. Known candidates such as MACHOs, dim red and white dwarfs, small black holes and neutrinos with mass can be tested against observations, so each must be shown unable to account for the dark matter before the simplest remaining explanation, WIMPs, is preferred.

exercises.prompt: If the dark matter in the Milky Way were composed entirely of MACHOs (evidence shows it is not), approximately how many would there have to be? Assume the average mass of a MACHO is 1/1000 that of the Sun, and that dark matter has a mass 10 times that of the luminous Milky Way galaxy with its $10^{11}$ stars of average mass 1.5 times the Sun’s mass.

answer.hint: Find the luminous mass in solar masses from the number of stars and their average mass, take ten times it for the dark matter, and divide by the mass of one MACHO, $10^{-3}$ solar masses.

exercises.prompt: Assume the average density of the universe is 0.1 of the critical density needed for closure. What is the average number of protons per cubic meter, assuming the universe is composed mostly of hydrogen?

answer.hint: Take one tenth of $10^{-26}\;\text{kg/m}^{3}$ and divide by the mass of a proton, $1.67\times 10^{-27}\;\text{kg}$.
